summaries.title: 2023_PMC10229756_Adverse_Events_Following_Immunization_Among_Children_Under_Two_
summaries.ehr_evidence: Data was collected using a pretested, semi-structured questionnaire that contained 20 questions regarding the socio-demographic characteristics of the participants, vaccination details, and the AEFI history of the child.
summaries.summary: Prospective community-based observational study assessing the incidence and pattern of adverse events following immunization (AEFI) among children under two years of age in Uttarakhand, North India.
key_findings: The incidence of AEFI was 33.0 per 100 doses of vaccines administered.
212 AEFIs were reported from 152 of 255 vaccinated subjects.
The most common AEFI was fever (101, 47.6%), followed by swelling at the injection site (53, 25.0%).
Pentavalent + OPV had the highest AEFI incidence (48.8 per 100 doses), followed by DPT + MR + OPV (46.6 per 100 doses).
No AEFI was reported after BCG + Hepatitis B + OPV administration.
No significant association of AEFI with age or gender was found (p > 0.05).
All reported AEFIs were minor, and no serious AEFIs were identified.
summaries.population: Children aged less than two years receiving vaccines under the Universal Immunization Program in Uttarakhand, North India
summaries.exposure_domain: Routine childhood vaccines (Pentavalent, OPV, IPV, DPT, MR, BCG, Hepatitis B)
limitations: Conducted in a single block, limiting generalizability.
Recall bias due to reliance on maternal history for AEFI identification.
Inability to attribute specific AEFIs to individual vaccines due to co-administration.
Small sample size due to declined participation and loss to follow-up, introducing potential selection bias.

summaries.title: 2026_PMC13100012_Coverage_and_associated_factors_of_inactivated_polio_vaccine_up
summaries.ehr_evidence: The current study was conducted based on the most recent Demographic and Health Survey (DHS) data of 20 Sub-Saharan African countries.
summaries.summary: Secondary data analysis assessing inactivated polio vaccine (IPV) coverage and determinants among children aged 12–23 months across 20 Sub-Saharan African countries using pooled DHS survey data.
key_findings: Pooled IPV coverage was 65.10% (95% CI: 55.44, 74.76).
Maternal age 20–35 years (AOR = 1.08, 95% CI: 1.00, 1.18) and >35 years (AOR = 1.22, 95% CI: 1.11, 1.34) were positively associated with IPV uptake.
Maternal education at primary (AOR = 1.30, 95% CI: 1.23, 1.37) and secondary+ levels (AOR = 1.87, 95% CI: 1.76, 1.99) increased odds.
Rich household wealth showed an inverse association (AOR = 0.84, 95% CI: 0.79, 0.89).

ANC visits 1–3 (AOR = 1.86, 95% CI: 1.72, 2.01) and ≥4 (AOR = 2.51, 95% CI: 2.33, 2.70), health facility delivery (AOR = 1.86, 95% CI: 1.77, 1.97), and PNC (AOR = 1.73, 95% CI: 1.65, 1.82) were significant positive determinants.
Urban residence (AOR = 1.24, 95% CI: 1.17, 1.31) and high community women's literacy (AOR = 1.68, 95% CI: 1.54, 1.83) were associated with higher uptake.
Regional disparities were observed, with Southern Africa showing the highest odds compared to Central Africa (AOR = 8.41, 95% CI: 7.08, 9.99).
summaries.study_design: cross-sectional secondary data analysis with multilevel logistic regression
summaries.population: children aged 12–23 months and their mothers in 20 Sub-Saharan African countries (weighted n=43,564)
summaries.exposure_domain: socio-demographic factors, maternal healthcare utilization, community-level characteristics, and geographic region
limitations: cross-sectional design prevents causal inference
reliance on verbal reports and vaccination cards may introduce recall bias
limited data on health system factors
potential time lag between data collection and publication

summaries.title: 2009_PMC2685976_A_liposome-based_mycobacterial_vaccine_induces_potent_adult_and_
summaries.ehr_evidence: Specific pathogen-free C57BL/6 mice (7 days of age (1-week-old, neonates) or 8–12 weeks old (adult), Charles River) were bred and kept under specific pathogen-free conditions in the university zootechnology unit.
summaries.summary: Preclinical murine study evaluating the immunogenicity, dendritic cell targeting, and protective efficacy of the CAF01 liposome-based adjuvant against tuberculosis in neonatal and adult mice.
key_findings: Ag85B-ESAT-6/CAF01 significantly reduced post-challenge M. bovis BCG bacterial counts in spleen and lungs compared to Alum control (p<0.05).
Ag85B-ESAT-6/Alum did not confer protective efficacy, with CFU counts as high as in unimmunized controls.
Twenty-four hours post-immunization, 84.2 ± 4.8% of adjuvant-bearing cells in adult draining lymph nodes were CD11c+ DCs.
The proportion of total DCs bearing antigen and adjuvant was low (0.09 ± 0.04%), translating to 523 ± 254 Ag+Adj+ DCs per adult mouse.
In neonates, adjuvant-bearing cells were 71.2 ± 9.8% CD11c+ DCs, with a lower Ag+Adj+ proportion (28.6 ± 8.6%) and count (151 ± 119 DCs per mouse).
Vaccine-associated DCs peaked around Day 5 and were not detected by Day 21 post-immunization.
CAF01 induced sustained adult-like Th1 (IFN-γ, TNF-α) and Th17 (IL-17) responses in neonates comparable to adults (p>0.05).
captured_features: Cytokine production (IFN-γ, TNF-α, IL-2, IL-17, IL-5)
Dendritic cell surface markers (CD11c, CD40, CD86, CD205)
Bacterial colony-forming units (CFU) in spleen and lungs
pathologies_diseases: Tuberculosis (Mycobacterium tuberculosis / M. bovis BCG infection)
summaries.study_design: Preclinical murine immunization and challenge model
summaries.population: C57BL/6 mice (neonates at 1 week of age and adults at 8-12 weeks)
limitations: Mouse model limitations in predicting human vaccine efficacy
Fluorochrome labeling intensity may not capture all labeled cell populations in vivo
Detection limits of the method may affect DC migration timing estimates
Short half-life of activated DCs complicates duration estimation of the phenomenon

summaries.title: 2012_PMC3469560_Attitudes_of_the_general_public_and_general_practitioners_in_fiv
summaries.ehr_evidence: In December 2009/January 2010 and April 2010, 500 randomly selected members of the general public in Germany, France, the United States, China, and Mexico were surveyed by telephone about vaccination for seasonal and A/H1N1 pandemic influenza. Also, in April 2010, 100 randomly selected general practitioners were surveyed.
summaries.summary: Cross-sectional survey of the general public and general practitioners in five countries examining attitudes, perceptions, and vaccination coverage rates for seasonal and A/H1N1 pandemic influenza during the 2009/2010 season.
key_findings: Adult A/H1N1 pandemic influenza vaccination coverage in Dec 2009/Jan 2010 was 12% in France, 11% in Germany, 41% in the US, 13% in Mexico, and 12% in China.
Adult seasonal influenza vaccination coverage in Dec 2009/Jan 2010 was 29% in France, 25% in Germany, 46% in the US, 30% in Mexico, and 10% in China.
Inclusion of the A/H1N1 pandemic strain increased willingness to be vaccinated for seasonal influenza in the US, Mexico, and China but not in Germany or France.
The 2009/2010 A/H1N1 pandemic increased seasonal influenza vaccine uptake in Mexico but had little effect in other countries.
GP recommendation was a common reason for receiving the pandemic vaccine, while lack of risk perception and safety concerns were common reasons for not being vaccinated.
summaries.population: general public (adults and parents) and general practitioners in France, Germany, the US, Mexico, and China
summaries.exposure_domain: influenza vaccination, pandemic/seasonal influenza exposure, media coverage, GP recommendations
limitations: small sample size (500 public, 100 GPs per country)
low survey response rates leading to potential selection bias
geographic limitation in China and Mexico (only 3 largest cities surveyed)
self-reported vaccination status subject to recall and honesty bias
cross-sectional design limits causal inference

summaries.title: 2014_PMC4256824_Determinants_of_vaccination_coverage_and_adherence_to_the_Greek_
summaries.ehr_evidence: The infant was considered as immunized or not based on the immunization card, as provided by the National Greek Health Care System.
summaries.summary: Cross-sectional survey evaluating vaccination coverage and socioeconomic determinants among infants aged 2-24 months in Athens, Greece during 2009-2011.
key_findings: 4.9% (95% CI 3.9%-6.0%) of parents admitted omitting a vaccine due to beliefs.
Infants were less likely to be fully vaccinated if they belonged to a minority group, had >1 sibling, young/illiterate parents, non-public insurance, or unemployed parents.
Appropriate hepatitis B immunization was strongly associated with hexavalent vaccine use (97.5% vs 54.2% at 6 months, 92.8% vs 25.7% at 12 months, p<0.01).
Multivariate analysis confirmed parental age, educational/occupational status, and family size (>3 children) as independent predictors of immunization status.
Lack of insurance was not associated with missed vaccine doses (57.8% vs 57.8%, p=NS).
summaries.population: infants aged 2-24 months visiting a tertiary public outpatient clinic in Athens, Greece (2009-2011)
summaries.exposure_domain: socioeconomic status, parental demographics, economic crisis period
limitations: convenience sample not representative of general population
overrepresentation of minority and low-SES children
underrepresentation of high-SES and rural families
less stringent criteria used to define complete vaccination
potential selection bias from outpatient clinic recruitment

summaries.title: 2013_PMC4515582_Are_Recent_Medical_Graduates_More_Skeptical_of_Vaccines
summaries.ehr_evidence: Surveys covering vaccine knowledge, attitudes, and beliefs were mailed in 2005 to 712 of these parent-identified providers.
summaries.summary: Cross-sectional survey investigating the association between US primary care provider graduation year and beliefs regarding vaccine safety, efficacy, and disease susceptibility.
key_findings: Recent graduates had 15% decreased odds of believing vaccines are efficacious compared to the preceding 5-year cohort (OR: 0.85, 95% CI: 0.73–0.99).
For every 5-year increase in graduation year, there was a 24% reduced odds of believing immunizations are one of the safest forms of medicine (OR: 0.76, 95% CI: 0.67–0.87).
Recent graduates had 1.3 times higher odds of believing immunizations do more harm than good (OR: 1.3, 95% CI: 1.0–1.8).
3.7% of recent graduates believed that immunizations do more harm than good.
Significant decreased odds of believing polio vaccines (IPV and OPV) were safe for recent compared to older graduates.
summaries.population: primary care health care providers in the United States
limitations: cross-sectional design prevents causal inference
graduation year used as proxy for age
non-representative sample nested within a case-control study
small sample size for some analyses
data collected in 2005 may not reflect current provider beliefs
limited patient sample per provider used to categorize exemption status

summaries.title: 2015_PMC4640112_Febrile_seizures_after_2009_influenza_A_H1N1_vaccination_and_inf
summaries.ehr_evidence: In addition to information from the national population registry, we used information from the Norwegian Directorate of Health, the Norwegian Surveillance System for Communicable Diseases, the Norwegian Immunisation Register, and the Norwegian Patient Register.
summaries.summary: Nationwide registry-based self-controlled case series study estimating the risk of febrile seizures in Norwegian children following 2009 H1N1 influenza vaccination or infection.
key_findings: The incidence rate ratio (IRR) of febrile seizures 1–3 days after vaccination was 2.00 (95% CI: 1.15–3.51).
No increased risk of febrile seizures was observed in the period 4–7 days after vaccination.
The IRR of febrile seizures on the same day as a diagnosis of influenza was 116.70 (95% CI: 62.81–216.90).
A tenfold increased risk was observed in the period 1–3 days after a diagnosis of influenza (IRR 10.12, 95% CI: 3.82–26.82).
summaries.population: 226,889 Norwegian children born 2006–2009 (up to 45 months old) resident in Norway as of October 1, 2009
limitations: Limited information on potential confounders
Lack of validity testing for outcome diagnosis
Under-ascertainment of influenza cases in primary care
Results likely apply to more severe influenza infections

summaries.title: 2014_PMC5779422_Human_papillomavirus_vaccination_coverage_among_adolescents_2007
summaries.ehr_evidence: CDC analyzed data from the 2007–2013 National Immunization Survey-Teen (NIS-Teen) and national postlicensure vaccine safety data among females and males.
summaries.summary: Assessment of HPV vaccination coverage among US adolescents aged 13–17 years from 2007–2013 and postlicensure safety monitoring from 2006–2014.
key_findings: Vaccination coverage with ≥1 dose increased from 53.8% (2012) to 57.3% (2013) among girls and from 20.8% (2012) to 34.6% (2013) among boys.
Receipt of ≥1 dose by age 13 increased by an average of 5.9% (95% CI = 2.8%–9.0%) with each new birth cohort, reaching 46.8% (95% CI = 41.2%–52.5%) for the 2000 cohort.
Missed vaccination opportunities ranged from 9.3% (95% CI = 8.1%–10.8%) for the 1994 cohort to 83.7% (95% CI = 77.8%–88.2%) for the 2000 cohort.
If missed opportunities were eliminated, coverage for the 2000 cohort could have reached 91.3% (95% CI = 87.9%–93.8%) by age 13.
VAERS received 25,176 adverse event reports post-HPV vaccination; 92.4% of HPV4 reports were classified as nonserious.
summaries.study_design: Cross-sectional survey analysis with birth cohort analysis and passive safety monitoring
summaries.population: Adolescents aged 13–17 years in the United States
limitations: Low cell phone household response rate (23.3%)
Incomplete provider-reported vaccination histories
Missed opportunity evaluation limited to encounters with other vaccinations
VAERS passive reporting cannot determine causality
Potential underreporting of adverse events

summaries.title: 2018_PMC5945909_Parents_attitudes_towards_topical_fluoride_and_vaccines_for_chil
summaries.ehr_evidence: We analyzed data collected from 2011 to 12 for 361 children from three Washington state dental clinics.
summaries.summary: Case-control study examining the overlap between parental attitudes and internet use regarding topical fluoride and vaccines, and their association with refusal of these preventive treatments.
key_findings: 51.5% of parents refused fluoride, only 27.7% reported refusing vaccinations.
Topical fluoride and vaccine refusal are modestly correlated (r = 0.23).
In adjusted models, only not using fluoride toothpaste was significantly associated with fluoride refusal (PR = 1.36, 95% CI 1.02–1.89).

For vaccine refusal, in the full adjusted model, vaccine safety concerns (PR = 1.81, 95% CI 1.49–2.20), internet use for vaccine information (PR = 2.84, 95% CI 2.09–3.87), and perceived severity of preventable cavities (PR = 1.29, 95% CI 1.04–1.60) remained significant predictors.
White respondents reported 62% higher likelihood of vaccine refusal (PR = 1.62, 95% CI 1.24–2.70).
summaries.population: 361 parents and children from three dental clinics in Washington state, USA
summaries.exposure_domain: Parental attitudes and internet use for health information
limitations: Limited to three dental clinics in Washington state
Vaccine refusal based on self-report
Lack of data on parental dental and medical history
Incomplete coverage of theoretical model domains

summaries.title: 2018_PMC6013082_Strategic_Response_to_an_Outbreak_of_Circulating_Vaccine-Derived
summaries.ehr_evidence: Data were derived from acute flaccid paralysis (AFP) case surveillance, stool specimen testing, administrative vaccination coverage records, and postcampaign monitoring surveys.
summaries.summary: Descriptive report of a circulating vaccine-derived poliovirus type 2 (cVDPV2) outbreak in Syria (2017–2018), detailing case epidemiology, surveillance performance, and the impact of monovalent OPV type 2 vaccination campaigns and environmental surveillance on interrupting transmission.
key_findings: 74 cVDPV2 cases were identified, with a median age of 15 months.
46 of 74 cases (62%) occurred in females.
30 cases (41%) occurred in children who had never received an OPV dose.
71 cases (96%) were reported from Deir-ez-Zor governorate.
Environmental sewage sampling and mOPV2 vaccination campaigns successfully interrupted cVDPV2 transmission.
summaries.population: children in Syria, primarily aged <5 years
limitations: subnational gaps in AFP surveillance performance
delays in receiving laboratory results due to transport and security constraints
administrative coverage denominators may not reflect actual population due to migration
postcampaign monitoring relies on parental recall

summaries.ehr_evidence: Questionnaires, in-depth interviews, and focus group discussions, as well as observations, were conducted before the campaign.
summaries.summary: Rapid qualitative anthropological assessment of oral cholera vaccine acceptability in Nampula, Mozambique, assessing barriers and levers for vaccine acceptance amid political resistance and mistrust.
key_findings: 95% of participants reported knowledge about cholera.
66% identified dirtiness as the principal cause of cholera.
26% reported previous negative experiences associated with immunization.
55% preferred injectable vaccines over oral delivery.
95% expressed willingness to be vaccinated.
83% preferred administration by health professionals rather than community health workers.
75% favored public health center-based delivery over home-based delivery.

summaries.ehr_evidence: Vaccination status was determined from the Australian Childhood Immunisation Register and deemed either “complete” (no doses overdue) or “incomplete” (1 or more doses overdue) at the time of questionnaire completion.
summaries.summary: Cross-sectional study assessing sociodemographic and parental belief factors associated with incomplete childhood vaccination status in Western Australia.
key_findings: 20% (116/589) of children had incomplete vaccination status.
Children with incomplete status were more likely born overseas (OR: 3.52, 95% CI: 1.54 to 8.05).
More likely to have a healthcare professional advise delaying or not vaccinating (OR: 4.25, 95% CI: 2.07 to 8.69).
Associated with lower parental education (<Year 10 high school) (OR: 2.92, 95% CI: 1.34 to 6.39).
Associated with larger family size (OR: 1.39 per child increase, 95% CI: 1.03 to 1.87).
No significant association between parental beliefs/attitudes and vaccination status remained after adjusting for sociodemographic factors.
summaries.population: children <6 years old attending outpatient clinics in Perth, Western Australia, and their parents

summaries.title: 2019_PMC6898916_The_maternal_antibody_against_diphtheria_tetanus_and_pertussis_s
summaries.ehr_evidence: In 2018, 200 neonates hospitalized in Shunyi Women and Children’s Hospital in Beijing, and 238 neonates hospitalized in Qianjiang Central Hospital located in the southwestern mountainous areas were included in this study.
summaries.summary: Cross-sectional serological study comparing maternal DTP vaccine-associated antibody levels in neonates from urban Beijing and rural Chongqing, China.
key_findings: Mean anti-Dtx IgG was significantly lower in Qianjiang (0.04 IU/ml) than Shunyi (0.12 IU/ml) (P < 0.0001).
Protective anti-Dtx prevalence was lower in Qianjiang (7.1%) than Shunyi (30.5%) (χ2 = 21.788, P < 0.0001).
Mean anti-Ttx IgG was significantly lower in Qianjiang (0.07 IU/ml) than Shunyi (0.18 IU/ml) (P < 0.0001).
Protective anti-Ttx prevalence was lower in Qianjiang (7.6%) than Shunyi (38.5%) (χ2 = 33.569, P < 0.0001).
No significant difference in mean anti-Ptx IgG between regions (P = 0.2395), but detectable rate was higher in Qianjiang (39.9%) than Shunyi (30.5%) (χ2=4.202, P=0.0404).
Two neonates from Qianjiang had anti-PT IgG ≥100.0 IU/ml, suggesting recent pertussis exposure in their mothers.
captured_features: serum antibody concentrations (anti-Dtx, anti-Ttx, anti-Ptx IgG)
summaries.population: 438 neonates (1-28 days old) hospitalized in two regional hospitals in China
summaries.exposure_domain: geographic region and regional vaccine coverage
limitations: sample size limited to two hospitals
lack of maternal vaccination status data
no maternal blood samples collected for direct comparison

summaries.ehr_evidence: Eligible Kansas guardians of children aged 9 - 17 years completed an online survey.
summaries.summary: Cross-sectional survey study assessing Kansas guardians' perceptions of HPV and the HPV vaccine, and the influence of social media messages on those perceptions and vaccination decisions.
key_findings: 57.9% (n=55) of guardians reported seeing information about HPV and the HPV vaccine on social media.

Guardians who saw HPV vaccine information on social media were significantly more likely to perceive the vaccine could kill their child compared to those who did not (M=2.50, SD=1.62 vs M=1.74, SD=0.85; t(79)=0.019).
Children of guardians with annual household income ≥$100,000 were significantly more likely to have received at least one HPV vaccine dose than children of guardians earning <$100,000 (p=0.003).
Higher HPV vaccine harm perception scores significantly predicted lower effectiveness perception scores (β=-0.451, R=0.620, F[1,57]=35.63, p<0.0001), explaining 38.5% of the variance.

summaries.ehr_evidence: four focus group discussions were conducted with 28 vaccine-hesitant parents on November 8 and 9, 2021, three weeks after the submission of Pfizer-BioNTech’ application to Health Canada for approval of its pediatric formulation of its COVID-19 vaccine.
summaries.summary: Qualitative study exploring drivers of COVID-19 vaccine hesitancy among parents of 5-11 year old children in Quebec using focus group discussions.
key_findings: Out of 28 participants, seven intended to vaccinate their child(ren) while the remaining were unsure or unwilling.
Parents perceived vaccination as unnecessary due to low child risk and were concerned about side effects and political pressure.
Focus group findings may not be representative of most parents due to recruitment of vaccine-hesitant participants.

key_findings: 3.5% of children aged 6 months–4 years had received ≥1 dose of COVID-19 vaccine.
59.3% of children were unvaccinated but parents were open to vaccination.
37.2% of children were unvaccinated and parents were reluctant to vaccinate.
Parental openness to vaccination was higher among parents of Asian (83.1%), Black (61.1%), and Hispanic (66.2%) children compared to White children (52.9%).
Parental openness was lower in rural areas (45.8%) than urban areas (64.1%).
Provider recommendation for vaccination was reported by 24.6% of unvaccinated children with open parents versus 62.7% of vaccinated children.
